planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring or early fall, giving the tree plenty of room for its eventual broad pyramidal form.

directions: Norway spruce is a fast-growing, densely branched European conifer that forms a broad pyramid of dark green needles and long, pendulous cones, widely planted across the northern United States as a windbreak, screen, and specimen tree. It is the parent species behind dozens of dwarf and weeping garden cultivars, but the straight species itself grows into an imposing full-sized forest tree 50 to 75 feet tall at maturity. Plant in full sun on deep, moist, well-drained soil and water regularly while young to establish a deep root system; established trees tolerate cold, wind, and short dry spells well. Give it generous spacing from buildings and other trees, since its mature spread can rival its height.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in fall or late winter into acidic, well-drained soil, and set at least two genetically distinct plants near each other for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Rabbiteye blueberry is the wild-type Southeastern US species behind the dozens of named rabbiteye cultivars already bred for larger fruit and extended harvest, but the straight species itself remains a tough, adaptable shrub well suited to naturalized plantings and wildlife gardens. It tolerates heat, humidity, and periods of drought far better than northern highbush blueberries, making it the backbone of commercial blueberry production across the Gulf South. Plant in full sun on acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat, and because it is self-incompatible, grow at least two unrelated plants to ensure good pollination and fruit set. Established plants need only an annual light pruning of old or crowded canes to stay productive.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and divide congested clumps every few years to keep foliage dense.

directions: Oshima sedge is the plain green, unvariegated Japanese species that gave rise to the many white- and gold-margined EverColor and Evergold-type cultivars already common in gardens, forming a tidy, arching evergreen clump of narrow glossy leaves. It handles the dappled shade of a woodland garden as well as brighter sites with consistent moisture, and keeps its foliage through winter in most of its hardiness range. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, watering regularly during the first season to establish, after which it tolerates brief dry spells. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain a dense, fountain-like habit.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
